item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – A los Yankees les quedan un par de días de calendario, pero los partidos que determinarán cómo se juzga esta temporada no llegarán hasta la próxima semana. Todo lo que ocurra de aquí a entonces es simplemente preparación para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana.
Con su próximo enfrentamiento de comodines contra los Medias Rojas ya confirmado oficialmente, los Yankees completaron el viernes otras 18 entradas de temporada regular, logrando dividir honores en una doble cartelera tras vencer 6-3 a los Orioles en el Yankee Stadium.
La victoria de Boston sobre los Cachorros en el primer partido de su doble cartelera aseguró el quinto puesto de clasificación y confirmó el duelo contra los Yankees, quienes se quedaron con el cuarto puesto. Será una reedición exacta de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana del año pasado, que los Yankees ganaron en tres partidos.
"Prefiero mil veces que sea aquí. Lo quiero en el Bronx", dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. "Lo quiero con nuestros aficionados. Creo que, sin duda, existe esa ventaja".
Tras recuperarse de una derrota por 10-2 —sufrida justo después de la ceremonia de homenaje a CC Sabathia en el Monument Park—, Ryan McMahon, Spencer Jones, Anthony Volpe, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos y Luis García Jr. impulsaron carreras para los Yankees, que además contaron con una alentadora actuación de relevo de tres entradas y 2/3 por parte de Will Warren.
Los Yankees aún no han anunciado quién abrirá el partido de Comodin del martes contra los Medias Rojas; el coach de lanzadores, Matt Blake, señaló que están evaluando si utilizar a Max Fried con descanso adicional o a Cam Schlittler —principal candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana—, quien llegaría con su descanso habitual para el primer encuentro.
Sin embargo, dado que Gerrit Cole y Carlos Rodón también figuran como posibles abridores para la postemporada, está previsto que Warren pase a desempeñar un papel en el bullpen durante octubre. Como era de esperar, el repertorio de Warren lució mejor desde el bullpen, incluyendo una recta de cuatro costuras que promedió 94.5 mph (0.8 mph más que su promedio de temporada). Warren permitió tres imparables y no otorgó bases por bolas, además de ponchar a siete bateadores.
McMahon inauguró el marcador en la quinta entrada con un doble impulsador ante el abridor de los Orioles, Brandon Young, quien lanzó cinco episodios. Jones conectó un sencillo productor frente a Josh Walker en el sexto inning, y más tarde en esa misma entrada, Volpe bateó un doble de terreno que impulsó dos carreras ante Anthony Núñez.
Ramos y García conectaron sencillos productores en la séptima entrada.

item.title: [mlb.com] Warren dominates out of 'pen in possible preview of playoff role

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The Yankees have a couple of days left on the schedule, but the ones that will determine how this season is judged won’t happen until next week. Everything that transpires between now and then is simply preparation for the American League Wild Card Series.
With their upcoming Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox officially locked in, the Yankees crossed off another 18 innings of regular-season action on Friday, securing a split of a single-admission doubleheader with a 6-3 victory over the Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
Boston’s victory over the Cubs in Game 1 of their doubleheader secured the No. 5 seed and confirmed a matchup with the Yankees, who claimed the No. 4 seed. It will be an exact rematch of last year’s AL Wild Card Series, which the Yankees won in three games.
“I’d much rather have it here. I want it in the Bronx,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “I want it with our fans. I think there’s certainly that advantage.”
Bouncing back after they followed CC Sabathia’s Monument Park enshrinement with a 10-2 loss, Ryan McMahon, Spencer Jones, Anthony Volpe, Heliot Ramos and Luis García Jr. all drove in runs for the Yankees, who logged an encouraging 3 2/3-inning relief outing from Will Warren.
The Yankees have yet to announce who will start Tuesday’s AL Wild Card Game against the Red Sox, with pitching coach Matt Blake saying that they are weighing Max Fried on extra rest against AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler, who would be on normal rest for the opener.
But with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón also in line as potential playoff starters, Warren is slated to transition to a bullpen role in October. Not surprisingly, Warren’s stuff played up out of the bullpen, including a four-seam fastball that averaged 94.5 mph – 0.8 mph more than his season average. Warren permitted three hits without a walk, striking out seven.
McMahon opened the scoring with a fifth-inning RBI double off Orioles starter Brandon Young, who worked five frames. Jones touched Josh Walker for a sixth-inning RBI single, and Volpe found the seats for a two-run ground-rule double facing Anthony Nunez later that inning.
Ramos and García each had an RBI single in the seventh.

item.content:encoded:
Ahead of the New York Yankees 4:05 P.M. EST start time against the Baltimore Orioles, manager Aaron Boone shares a tidbit of what the pitching plan is heading into the Wild Card Series.
The series is best-of-three, meaning the Yankees will only need three starters instead of their usual five. While the starters haven't been officially named, it's fair to assume that Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Gerrit Cole will be their go-to guys.
Leaving Carlos Rodón with his role unknown. However, Boone said there has been much conversation on how to fit him in.
Aaron Boone Says That Carlos Rodón Will Likely Be Used Out of the Bullpen During Yankees Wild Card Series
The New York Yankees have a platoon of starting pitchers on their 40-man roster. However, the injury bug made a home within the Yankees pitchers this season, leaving their bullpen slightly scarce.
Carlos Rodón is one of the many Yankees players who dealt with an injury this season, but he is back and ready to be used out of the bullpen.
"Aaron Boone said that using Carlos Rodón out of the bullpen 'is a consideration' for the Wild Card round," Yankees beat writer Gary Phillips wrote on X. "Generally speaking, the lefty is 'very much in the conversation, deservedly so,' the #Yankees skipper said."
Aaron Boone said that using Carlos Rodón out of the bullpen “is a consideration” for the Wild Card round. Generally speaking, the lefty is “very much in the conversation, deservedly so,” the #Yankees skipper said.
— Gary Phillips (@GaryHPhillips) September 25, 2026
Rodón made his final start of the season on Tuesday and threw an absolute gem against the Tampa Bay Rays.
"Carlos Rodón hurled eight scoreless innings in a must-win game for the #Yankees, who did just that with a 2-0 victory over the Rays," New York sports reporter Peter Sblendorio wrote on X. "That's a season-high IP for Rodón, who picked up his 100th win and 1,500th strikeout. He is 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA this season."
Carlos Rodon hurled eight scoreless innings in a must-win game for the #Yankees, who did just that with a 2-0 victory over the Rays.
That’s a season-high IP for Rodon, who picked up his 100th win and 1,500th strikeout.
He is 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA this season.
— Peter Sblendorio (@petersblendorio) September 22, 2026
Along with Rodón, the Yankees have the option to utilize starter Will Warren out of the bullpen.
Yankees Could Face Boston Red Sox For Second Year in a Row
While the Yankees Wild Card opponent has yet to be determined, it will likely be their rival for the second straight year.
The Boston Red Sox will clinch the No. 5 seed with a win or a Chicago White Sox loss tonight.
The Red Sox lost to the Guardians, so they will not clinch the No. 5 seed today.
That means the #Yankees opponent in the Wild Card series remains TBD, officially. The next Red Sox win or White Sox loss would book NYY vs. BOS for a second consecutive year.
— Peter Sblendorio (@petersblendorio) September 25, 2026
"The Red Sox lost to the Guardians, so they will not clinch the No. 5 seed today," Sblendorio wrote on X. "That means the #Yankees opponent in the Wild Card series remains TBD, officially. The next Red Sox win or White Sox loss would book NYY vs. BOS for a second consecutive year."
This series will mark the seventh postseason meeting between the two historic franchises.
The Yankees currently came out on top this season with a 7-6 record over the Red Sox. In the postseason, they're tied 3-3 on series wins, but the Yankees have a slight edge with games won.

item.content:encoded:
With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.
Key takeaways
- Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
- Aaron Boone addressed conflicting media reports regarding Aaron Judge’s status.
- New York projects Gerrit Cole to lead its postseason starting rotation.

item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler made his final start of the regular season Thursday night.
Will his next be in Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday?




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
The Yankees aren’t saying and insist they haven’t decided on their postseason rotation with less than a week to go before the playoffs start.
Before a 6-4 comeback victory over the Rays at the Stadium, pitching coach Matt Blake said that Max Fried is in “heavy consideration” to pitch Game 1 on Tuesday, while Schlittler — who threw 70 pitches in an intentionally abbreviated outing against Tampa Bay — was also in the mix.
And Gerrit Cole, according to Blake, isn’t guaranteed a start in the wild-card series.
With Schlittler and Fried seemingly locked in to a start, Blake said Game 3 would go to Cole or Carlos Rodón.
“Both guys have pitched well down the stretch,’’ Blake said of Cole and Rodón. “All four guys are good options. It’s just a matter of making sure we check in, see where they’re at and finding the best fit for whoever we play.”
Their opponent is still undetermined, as Boston was unable to clinch the fifth spot in the American League after losing to Cleveland on Thursday.
Regardless of who the Yankees end up playing, part of the equation with the rotation will be rest, since Schlittler would be pitching on his fifth day if he went in Game 1 on Tuesday in The Bronx.
Cole, another option, would be on his sixth day, while Fried — as well as Rodón — would be on his seventh day.
Asked if they could be overthinking the situation by not just naming Schlittler the Game 1 starter after his Cy Young-worthy season, Blake said, “Certainly.”
Schlittler finished his first full year in the majors with an AL-best 1.95 ERA, as well as 239 strikeouts.
The ERA is third best in franchise history, trailing only Spud Chandler (1.64 in 1943) and Ron Guidry (1.74 in 1978).
“He’s earned the right to pitch Game 1,’’ Blake said prior to Schlittler’s final outing, in which he allowed two runs, one earned, in a meaningless game. “We’re taking inventory of all our starters and giving us the best chance to advance in the three-game series.”
And that could leave Cole out and ready for a potential ALDS matchup against the Rays.
“If we don’t have him as one of our three starters or out of the pen, he’d be available for [ALDS],’’ Blake said. “I don’t know where we’d go.”
Shop Yankees Merch
Blake said they could go with all four starters on the wild-card roster, understanding the challenges of putting those pitchers in an unfamiliar role.
“Any of those guys that haven’t pitched out of the pen in a while, you’ve got to make sure you’ve got a clear plan for them and they understand what role they’ll be in because you probably get one shot if we use one of these starters out of the pen,’’ Blake said. “They’re not gonna pitch two games [in the series].”

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – Arropado profundamente dentro de una sudadera con capucha, Cam Schlittler se desplazaba por el clubhouse de los Yankees a primeras horas de la tarde del jueves, con una tableta de video afianzada en su mano derecha. Lucía la expresión firme de alguien enfocado en el futuro, no del todo listo para celebrar el final de una campaña con calibre de Premio Cy Young.
Sin embargo, este es un momento tan bueno como cualquier otro para apreciar el panorama. Schlittler le puso los toques finales a sus estadísticas con tres sólidas entradas en la victoria de Nueva York por 6-4 sobre los Rays, terminando con efectividad de 1.95 para ganarse un lugar entre los mejores rendimientos en una sola temporada en la historia de los Yankees.
Solo Spud Chandler (1.64 en 1943) y Ron Guidry (1.74 in 1978) han registrado una mejor efectividad en la historia de la franquicia que Schlittler, quien permitió dos carreras (una limpia) y tres hits a lo largo de tres episodios.
La efectividad de 1.95 de Schlittler es la mejor en la Liga Americana desde que Justin Verlander registró efectividad de 1.75 por los Astros en el 2022.
Los Bombarderos mantuvieron la cuenta de pitcheos de Schlittler a 70 en su 33ra presentación y última de la campaña regular, preparando al diestro para una asignación como abridor en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Aunque algunos anticipaban que fuera una certeza que el favorito al Cy Young abriera el Juego 1, el club de Nueva York está contemplando la idea de que Schlittler en vez lance en el Juego 2. El zurdo Max Fried está recibiendo una fuerte consideración para la asignación del primer compromiso, según el coach de pitcheo Matt Blake.
Schlittler ponchó a cinco bateadores de los Rays, terminando la temporada regular con 239 ponches. Eso lo empata con Jack Chesbro (239 en 1904) en la cuarta mayor cantidad para un jugador de los Yankees en una misma temporada; solo Gerrit Cole (257 en el 2022, 243 en el 2021) y Guidry (248 en 1978) han conseguido más.
Considerado hombro a hombro con Dylan Cease de los Azulejos durante gran parte de la campaña en el debate del Cy Young, Schlittler se apartó con un sólido cierre. Registró efectividad de 1.17 (10 carreras, siete limpias) en sus últimas nueve aperturas, a lo largo de 54 episodios.
Schlittler permitió apenas 27 imparables y 18 boletos a lo largo de ese trecho, que se remonta al 9 de agosto contra Atlanta, ponchando a 68. Se convertiría en el séptimo jugador de los Yankees en ganar el Premio Cy Young y el primero desde Cole en el 2023.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have already confirmed their postseason path with a Wild Card series at home against the Boston Red Sox. Most fans assumed that American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler will start Game 1 since he's arguably the best pitcher in all of MLB this season. However, Yankees manager Aaron Boone recently claimed he's unsure of the order with Schlittler and Max Fried starting the first two in some order.
MLB insider Bryan Hoch revealed Boone is not lying and transcribed pitching coach Matt Blake sharing the Yankees are considering Fried over Schlittler for Game 1:
"I think it's more just getting all the information after his last outing here and making sure he's in a good spot to go on five days again. Max is on extended rest, and Cam would be on his third five day in a row. So just making sure he's in a good spot before we make any rash decisions."
Fried having extra rest is one reason given, but it still has Yankees fans on edge. The season has seen Fried hit with injuries for many months and having a shorter pitches limit in recent months. Schlittler is obviously the top pitcher for New York, but many fans trust Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon more than Fried right now.
Another Reason For Max Fried Yankees Won't Admit
One logical reason for Fried starting Game 1 would be the Yankees wanting a fully rested bullpen to enhance their chances. Fried has not thrown more than 100 pitches since May 3rd against the Baltimore Orioles.
Boone could view Fried as a trustworthy arm he may want to pull after 4 or 5 innings to start maneuvering bullpen matchups against top Red Sox hitters like Willson Contreras and Wilyer Abreu. This scenario would see Schlittler saved for Game 2 with fewer bullpen arms ready to go.
The reaction to this potential plan has been overwhelmingly negative in Yankees fan spaces since it feels like overthinking too much. History sees the best pitcher starting Game 1, and Sonny Gray is the expected starter for Boston since he's been the top starter all year. Boone is under fire to make the right decision here.
Yankees Will Likely Still Start Cam Schlittler
The logic of Fried having extra rest means little since Schlittler would be on his normal rest ahead of Game 1. Aaron Boone is expected to manage Schlittler's pitches and remove him after a few innings of limited work.
Game 3 remains the biggest question if the Yankees and Red Sox split the first two to set up a winner takes all scenario. Cole has the track record of being a legendary pitcher throughout his long career with the Yankees, Houston Astros and Pittsburgh Pirates.
Rodon has been on fire and looks better than ever since returning from injury. Boone will likely trust Cole more due to his history in big games. The Yankees must get by the rival Red Sox to enter the real playoffs with teams like Tampa Bay, the Cleveland Guardians and Texas Rangers in their way.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Why Yankees Are Considering Max Fried For Game 1 Vs Red Sox appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees Sequence of the Week: Carlos Rodón (9/22)

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees were officially eliminated from the AL East title race by the Rays’ win in the second game of the doubleheader on Tuesday. They managed to temporarily stave off elimination thanks to a dominant performance by Carlos Rodón in the first game of the day’s twin billing. With eight scoreless innings, he equalled his longest outing in a Yankees uniform to lower his season ERA to a sterling 2.67. Given the gravity of the performance and the game, it was a no-brainer to select Rodón for our Sequence of the Week.
We join Rodón facing Liam Hicks to lead off the top of the second. With one of MLB’s best run suppressors in Nick Martinez on the mound for the Rays, the task ahead of Rodón is a tough one. Hicks has proven an inspired pickup from the Marlins by the Rays at the deadline, batting .305 with a 143 wRC+ in 123 plate appearances since making the switch from the Atlantic Coast to the Gulf Coast, which explains why the catcher is batting cleanup for Tampa Bay.
Rodón starts Hicks with a first pitch four-seamer at 93 mph, Ali Sánchez setting a target low and away.
Rodón nails his spot with this fastball, painting the corner for called strike one. Hicks must be looking for something on the inner half, because he watches it go by without a thought of offering.
It appears Rodón is satisfied with the way that pitch felt coming out of the hand, because he goes right back to that pitch-location combo.
Same pitch, even better execution. Rodón paints the bottom edge of the zone with this 93 mph four-seamer for strike two called. It’s obvious at this point that Hicks is hunting something he can pull given the bat has not left his shoulder, and this is the last pitch you want to be trying to get out in front of.
At this point, Hicks has to defend that corner of the strike zone. Establishing the four-seamer for called strikes there has Hicks perfectly set up for the wipeout slider down and away out of the zone as he’s now forced to look away.
It’s the right idea but just without the execution to match. Rodón pulls this slider a hair, bouncing it beyond home plate for ball one. It looks like a ball low out of the hand, making for a pretty easy take from Hicks.
Rodón is still in the driver’s seat with the count 1-2. He’d be well within his rights to try another slider low and away, this time trying to execute it closer to the zone. However, he elects to go back to the four-seamer, if not for the strikeout then to set up a future slider.
Even though Rodón fails to elevate this four-seamer where he wants it and ends up leaving it in a pretty dangerous place, the 19 inches of induced vertical break keep the pitch above Hicks’ barrel, leading to a foul ball rather than a ball in play. What’s more, as we are about to see, this fastball is the perfect setup pitch for a chase slider.
By continuing to prove that he can land his four-seamer on the outer edge of the zone, Rodón keeps the door open for Hicks to chase a slider.
Rodón unleashes a dandy, this slider looking like a strike out of the hand before falling off the table for the swinging strikeout. This kind of slider is so tough to lay off because it remains over the plate for the entire journey toward home, the sharp downward movement carrying it into an unhittable location. Rodón can thank the prior four-seamer for the outcome of this slider.
Look at the way the slider and the four-seamer that immediately preceded it look exactly the same coming out of Rodón’s hand. Rodón landing that four-seamer where he did set a perfect target for him to tunnel the subsequent slider. Hicks really never had a chance at distinguishing the two pitches from each other and goes down with a weak hack.
Here’s the full sequence:
Rodón is hitting his stride just in time for the playoffs. Over his last eight starts he has a 1.67 ERA with less than one home run allowed per nine, allowing two or fewer runs in all eight of those appearances. He really can’t do much more when it comes to making a case for the postseason rotation. The competition is fierce, with Cy Young frontunner Cam Schlittler starting early on and Aaron Boone looking likely to pick 2024 ace Gerrit Cole and 2025 ace Max Fried for the two other Wild Card Series starts. Even with Rodón’s recent excellence, he could be out of luck unless they advance. Still, Rodón has certainly earned the opportunity and is someone I would absolutely feel confident handing the ball.
We’ve written a lot about Rodón’s evolution as a starting pitcher to being a more well-rounded complete package thanks to the mastery of changeup and sinker. I certainly do not want to downplay this transformation and how key it is for his longevity. However, this outing was something of a throwback start for Rodón — a glimpse of the peak version from his days in Chicago and San Francisco. He whiffed over 30-percent of batters on his four-seamer and over 40-percent on his slider, that deadly pitch pairing the hallmark of his earlier years. This AB in particular was vintage Rodón, with each four-seamer exhibiting at least 19 inches of induced vertical break — well above the threshold that is considered elite — and his slider dropping two inches more than its season average. If he can hold onto the feel of this start, the Yankees will have a real weapon in the playoffs, be that out of the rotation or the bullpen.

item.content:encoded:
Judge hopes to be ready for playoffs and Stanton could return for Yankees after 5 1/2-month absence
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees slugger Aaron Judge hopes to return from a strained right calf for the playoffs next week and Giancarlo Stanton could be back after a 5 1/2-month absence.
New York manager Aaron Boone repeated he’s not counting on Judge to play in the AL Wild Card Series opener Tuesday. Judge, sidelined since Sept. 16, said he’s trying to do all he can to be in the lineup.
“The Bronx is a magical place in October,” Judge said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win over AL East champion Tampa Bay. “I don’t want to miss out on that opportunity.”
Judge had a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday. He was sidelined by a fractured rib from May 31 to Sept. 8 and played in just seven games before the latest injury.
“Any injection doesn’t feel too good that day, but I feel a lot better today and we’re going to keep making strides,” he said.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge is hitting .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS in 66 games this season, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs since coming back from the rib injury.
“We are going to listen to the body and see how he heals,” Boone said. “If he is in a position to do that, obviously we are going to want him. So, no, I haven’t ruled anything out, of course.”
Boone said Tuesday he wasn’t planning on having Judge available for next week’s best-of-three series, likely against Boston.
“Obviously as a player, you don’t want to hear that but that’s out of my control,” Judge said.
Boone said Judge had a moderate strain.
“Everybody’s `moderate’ is a little different,” Judge said.
Stanton, trying to return from injuries to calf muscles in both legs, faced pitchers Wednesday at Double-A Somerset along with center fielder Trent Grisham, sidelined since straining his right hamstring on Sept. 4. Both ran the bases and Stanton homered while taking six or seven at-bats.
“Putting them on the outskirts of the conversation,” Boone, bothered by a cold, said in a raspy voice.
Following the end of the seasons for Yankees farm teams, New York has minor leaguers working out at Somerset in nearby New Jersey.
Stanton hasn’t played since April 24 because of strained calf muscles in both legs after starting the season with a .256 batting average, three homers and 14 RBIs in 24 games. The 36-year-old former NL MVP had 38 homers and 100 RBIs in his first season with New York in 2018 but has missed 500 of 1,194 games since (41.9%), through the end of this regular season.
His other injuries included strains of his right biceps, right knee, left hamstring (three times), left quadriceps and both calf muscles along with right ankle inflammation, left Achilles tendinitis and tendon pain in both elbows.
“You’re looking more at a pinch-hit scenario,” Boone said. “We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option.”
Stanton is owed $25 million next year in the final guaranteed season of a $325 million, 13-year contract that includes a $10 million buyout of a 2028 club option.
Lagrange could be brought up for major league debut
Carlos Lagrange, a 23-year-old right-hander who reached 100 mph with 98 pitches at Triple-A this year, threw to batters at Somerset. He was out between June 28 and Sept. 16 because of a right capsule strain.
Lagrange was shifted to the bullpen at the start of June.
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said.
Clarke Schmidt still out
Right-hander Clarke Schmidt, who returned Sept. 16 following Tommy John surgery in July 2025, played catch but remains sidelined by right biceps cramps. New York had hoped to use him as a reliever in the postseason.
“Today was better than yesterday,” Boone said. “If he’s not a real viable option by tomorrow, then we’ll probably go a different way.”
Postseason rotation
Boone said Cam Schlitter will start Game 1 or 2 of the playoffs. Max Fried appears set to start whichever game Schlittler doesn’t, with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón available for Game 3.
“Whoever goes 1 or 2 can pitch 2 and 5 in the next series,” Boone said.
Fernando Cruz throws a bullpen
Right-hander Fernando Cruz threw a bullpen this week and is to throw another one Thursday.
He hasn’t pitched in a game since Aug. 25 because of right elbow discomfort caused by a partially torn ulnar collateral ligament.
“I’m in a really good position to be back I will say in the next couple of weeks,” Cruz said.
He took issue with the diagnosis of his injury.
“I had a real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” he said. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart it’s not a partial tear.”
Volpe will see time at the hot corner
With second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. back from a sprained right thumb, Boone said Anthony Volpe will see time at third.
“I’ll probably get him on there a time or two,” Boone said.
Volpe entered Wednesday hitting .263 with one homer, seven RBIs and four stolen bases over 11 games since his recall from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. He played three games at third base for the RailRiders.
“It didn’t feel that bad when I played there, but we’ll see,” Volpe said.

item.title: [Fox News] Why Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is in the AL MVP conversation and could join an exclusive club
item.dc:creator: Ryan Canfield
item.description: If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon. The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award. But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the sa
item.content:encoded:
If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon.
The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award.
But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the same season.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Heading into his final start of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday, Schlittler leads all American League pitchers in ERA (1.94) and is tied for first in WHIP with Drew Rasmussen (0.91). He has been durable, making all his starts, and is second in the AL in innings pitched (190 2/3).
With a devastating combination of cutters, sinkers and fastballs, the young right-hander has racked up 234 strikeouts, third in the AL behind Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams (244) and likely Cy Young runner-up Dylan Cease (239).
Schlittler has set a Yankees franchise record by allowing one or no runs in 21 starts this year. He became just the third pitcher age 25 or younger in the live-ball era, which began in 1920, to achieve the feat, joining Dean Chance (1964) and Blake Snell (2018).
Schlittler also leads the AL in bWAR with 7.0, ahead of other MVP contenders such as Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez (6.6), Kansas City Royals star Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Rays phenom Junior Caminero (5.6).
The numbers for Schlittler are outstanding, but they don’t tell the full story.
Schlittler has been the pillar of the Yankees' pitching staff, which leads all of baseball with a 3.21 team ERA.
While the pitching staff has been fantastic, it has have dealt with plenty of injuries to the starting rotation.
Gerrit Cole didn’t make his season debut until May 22, as he was recovering from Tommy John surgery. Carlos Rodón began the season on the IL after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur and loose bodies and didn’t debut until May 10. That was just his first stint on the IL. He returned to the IL on July 3 and didn’t come back until Aug. 18.
Rodón was not the only Yankees ace to land on the IL twice, as Max Fried did as well. Fried first went on the IL with a left elbow bone bruise on May 13, right after Cole returned, and was activated on July 22. He went on the IL for a second time on Aug. 17 with the same injury and returned Aug. 29.
Ryan Weathers, who had been key in stepping up during the absences of Cole, Fried and Rodón, went on the IL on Aug. 23 with a left forearm flexor strain.
For the Yankees, not only was it paramount that Schlittler make every start, but it was also essential that he remain dominant to help keep the rotation afloat.
Adding to the pressure on Schlittler and the pitching staff as a whole, the Yankees’ offense cratered after Aaron Judge was placed on the IL at the beginning of June. Since June 1, the Yankees have hit a paltry .229 with a putrid .297 on-base percentage.
The Yankees’ offensive ineptitude put further pressure on Schlittler and Co. to win games without Judge.
In 2023, the Yankees’ season went off the rails when Judge suffered a torn ligament in his toe. They went 25-31 without the captain and missed the postseason. The Yankees’ pitching staff in 2023, led by Cole, who won the AL Cy Young Award that season, had a 3.97 ERA, which was not enough to save the Yankees from finishing 82-80.
In 2026, the Yankees went 48-41 without Judge in the lineup, buoyed by the pitching staff’s excellence. Carried by the Schlittler-led pitching staff, the Yankees made the postseason and secured home-field advantage in the American League Wild Card Series.
While the Yankees didn’t catch the Tampa Bay Rays and win the American League East, they might have missed the postseason entirely if it weren’t for Schlittler.
By the award’s definition, Schlittler has been the most valuable player on his team.
Alvarez has been dominant in his own right. The hulking left-handed hitter, with a .316 batting average, 41 home runs and 102 RBI made a bid for the Triple Crown, but that seems out of reach.
Alvarez has been primarily a designated hitter, filling that role in 131 of the 154 games he played this season. Shohei Ohtani is the only player to win an MVP as a primary designated hitter, and he did so after becoming the first player to hit 50 home runs and steal 50 bases in a season.
Unless Alvarez surges to win the Triple Crown, nothing he is doing this season is unprecedented or historic.
Alvarez’s Astros, who are 78-80, might miss the postseason despite playing in the American League West, a division that has been historically bad.
Bobby Witt Jr. has been his usual superstar self but missed 11 games due to injury and has also taken a slight step back from last season while playing for the AL Central-worst Kansas City Royals.Caminero, the linchpin of the AL-leading Rays’ lineup, trails Schlittler in bWAR by more than a full win. Still, his .274 average and 41 home runs leave him in the thick of the AL MVP race.
Despite the excellence of Alvarez, Witt and Caminero, Schlittler should become the first pitcher since Justin Verlander in 2011 to win the American League MVP.
Verlander, like Schlittler this year, led the American League in bWAR with 8.6.
Without Schlittler, the Yankees do not survive Judge’s absence. When the Yankees could hardly scrape together three runs a game in the dead of summer, Schlittler made sure it was enough to hold on.
Without Schlittler’s dominance and durability, the Yankees do not have the second-best record in the American League (91-67).
Without Schlittler, Yankees fans are in a complete state of panic because they might still be trying to secure a Wild Card berth in a weak American League.
At the sportsbooks, Schlittler is a long shot to win the American League MVP. But odds be damned, the award should be his. He has landed on the moon.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Projecting the Yankees' playoff bullpen trust tree behind Headrick, Blackburn, Bednar
item.dc:creator: Pat Ragazzo
item.description: The New York Yankees have three main arms in their bullpen who they can rely on during the postseason. This trio of relievers consists of closer David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, the Yankees' best relief assets all season. But who can they count on in the trust tree behind these three relief pitchers? Let's try to project which bullpen arms the Yankees can lean on in the playoffs from most to least trustworthy. Yankees' most trustworthy relievers as playoffs approach Yankees manag
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have three main arms in their bullpen who they can rely on during the postseason. This trio of relievers consists of closer David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, the Yankees' best relief assets all season.
But who can they count on in the trust tree behind these three relief pitchers? Let's try to project which bullpen arms the Yankees can lean on in the playoffs from most to least trustworthy.
Yankees' most trustworthy relievers as playoffs approach
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has Bednar, Headrick and Blackburn, who he can go to in the late innings if the team has the lead or is in a tie game. But the Yankees are going to need more than that if they're going to make a deep run.
This is where Will Warren will likely come in as someone that can give the Yankees some key innings in long relief in the playoffs. Warren has not allowed a run in three innings as a reliever this season, and has pitched well as of late overall (2.45 ERA in September).
Hear me out on this next one: If Tim Hill makes the postseason roster, he will step up for the Yankees. Hill has allowed just one earned run across 11.1 playoff innings for the Yankees in the last two years. Since May 31, Hill has seen his ERA balloon from 2.53 to 4.71. But he is postseason tested, which means Boone and the Yankees should be able to count on him.
Last but not least, the sixth most trustworthy bullpen option could be newcomer John Schreiber. The right-hander has a 2.00 ERA over nine innings since joining the Yankees at the beginning of the month. Like Hill, Schreiber has postseason success, posting five scoreless relief appearances against the Yankees, ironically, in the 2024 postseason while pitching for the Kansas City Royals.
Who the Yankees shouldn't trust in ther playoff bullpen
Now we get to the part, where the names on this list probably should be pitching in lower leverage spots in the postseason. Fernando Cruz would've been included here, but his return is in doubt due to a partially torn UCL in his right elbow. Beyond Cruz, there is a pair of starters who are coming back from injury that likely can't be trusted at this point.
No. 1 is Clarke Schmidt, who just experienced biceps soreness when trying to warm up in the bullpen on Sunday. Schmidt came back from 2025 Tommy John surgery on September 16, but has been limited to one appearance, where he recorded two outs. It's hard to see how he could be high up on the trust tree in the postseason if the Yankees keep him on the playoff roster.
The second starter is Ryan Weathers, who had a breakout season for the Yankees this year. The expectation was that Weathers could be a solid relief option in the playoffs, but he is now unlikely to return in the regular season due to his left forearm flexor strain. It's difficult to envision Weathers coming back healthy at this point and being a trusted reliever in the biggest games of the year.
Should the Yankees choose to go: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Bednar, Headrick, Blackburn, Warren, Hill, Schreiber, Weathers, Schmidt, that would mean there's one more spot available for a pitcher on a 13-man staff. This last slot would come down to: Luis Gil, Michael Fulmer or Ryan Yarbrough.
While Gil has the most upside of the three, he can be erratic with his command at times. He also has a 6.75 ERA for his career in the postseason. Fulmer has a 4.50 ERA since joining the Yankees last month and Yarbrough is better suited to give length when the team is trailing. Whoever the Yankees decide to give the last spot to will be a low leverage option and at the bottom of the trust tree.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] 3 surprising players who could crash Yankees' playoff roster in Wild Card round
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: Despite their best efforts, the New York Yankees are all but guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series. Like any time the two heated rivals face off against each other, the three-game set will almost certainly push both teams to do whatever it takes to gain an advantage. For the Yankees, that could mean adding a few surprising players on the roster that you might not expect. With the Yankees nearly a lock to play the Red Sox, manager Aaron Boone has already been eyeing his li
item.content:encoded:
Despite their best efforts, the New York Yankees are all but guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series. Like any time the two heated rivals face off against each other, the three-game set will almost certainly push both teams to do whatever it takes to gain an advantage. For the Yankees, that could mean adding a few surprising players on the roster that you might not expect.
With the Yankees nearly a lock to play the Red Sox, manager Aaron Boone has already been eyeing his likely starting rotation in preparation for the postseason. The Yankees will likely roll with a combination of Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Gerrit Cole. That rotation would likely lead to some creativity when it comes to how the rest of the roster is constructed.
That creativity could potentially be used exclusively within the team’s bullpen. Would that mean that Carlos Rodón is left off the roster for the short series in favor of a pitcher more capable of coming out of the pen? With plenty of tough innings between the Yankees and Red Sox coming up, there could be some surprise arms out of the bullpen to bridge the gap between the starters and closer David Bednar.
3 surprise pitchers who could give the Yankees valuable innings in the postseason
Over the last few weeks of the season, relievers Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn have seemed to be feeling the effects of a long season where they have each thrown more than 77 innings. With that wear and tear weighing on their shoulders, they have both looked a little more human as of late. That doesn’t mean that they won’t step up when it matters the most in the postseason, but they may need some help.
The Yankees will need to collect at least 54 outs against the Red Sox in order to move on to the Divisional round. When it comes to the postseason, it doesn’t matter how you get those outs. In fact, it doesn’t even matter who gets those outs for you. For the Yankees, they could be giving the ball to a few pitchers that may turn some heads.
Ryan Weathers
While his battle with a nagging elbow flexor strain could complicate things, Ryan Weathers has the potential to become a game-changing pitcher for the Yankees in the Wild Card round. Out since August, Weathers may not come back in time to finish out the regular season. With the Yankees’ first postseason game scheduled for September 29, that doesn’t leave a lot of time for Weathers to make it back for a matchup against the Red Sox, either.
But if he can bounce back and throw an inning or two, Weathers may become one of the team’s most valuable weapons out of the pen. With a 9.4 K/9 rate this season, the southpaw is more than capable of picking up a much-needed punchout to quell a potential rally. Perhaps more importantly, he’s induced nine ground ball double plays in high-leverage situations this season.
If healthy enough to pitch, Weathers could be an effective option for Boone. That would go a long way toward saving relievers like Headrick and Blackburn for the later innings if needed.
Yerry de los Santos
With only three games to worry about in the Wild Card round, Boone could easily look to add as many versatile relievers as possible. Yerry de los Santos may not be the first name you'd think of when considering a lockdown postseason bullpen, but he could become a valuable arm against the Red Sox.
His propensity to fill the base paths with runners isn't exactly the best formula for postseason success. With a career WHIP of 1.334, it would be very unlikely that Boone would turn to de los Santos in a close game. But in the event of a blowout in either of the first two games, de los Santos would become the best option to eat innings and save the high-leverage arms for the next day. That could be invaluable in the long run.
With a high ground ball rate and an ability to miss barrels, de los Santos has been good at limiting the damage during his time with the Yankees. That could continue against the Red Sox. Just don't expect to see him jogging in from the bullpen in a tight one (even though he was briefly RP4, almost by default, in mid-August).
Elmer Rodriguez
After looking like a whole new pitcher following his most recent call up in August, Elmer Rodriguez offered fans a glimpse into his future as a postseason starter. Maybe just not this year, though. But that doesn't mean he won't be a big factor in the Wild Card round.
With an impressive combination of a power sinker and a four-seamer, Rodriguez is capable of getting ahead of hitters and establishing his fastball. This could allow him to set up his strong offering of breaking balls. On the season, batters are slugging just .182 off the sweeper and an embarrassingly low .091 off of his curveball.
As a short relief option, Rodriguez could see an uptick in velocity that would better play off of his breaking balls. With wipeout stuff, Rodriguez could be yet another surprise weapon for Boone to unleash out of the bullpen.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] No Yankees starter has had a better season than Ron Guidry. He marvels at Cam Schlittler
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: Clad in a black tux and a matching bowtie, Ron Guidry stepped to the podium at the New York Hilton Midtown on Jan. 27, 2024 to recognize a fellow Yankee and to pass a torch. Speaking at the Baseball Writers’ Association of America Awards Dinner in his Louisiana drawl, “Gator” introduced Gerrit Cole, voted the American League’s Cy Young for 2023. Guidry won the same award while wearing pinstripes back in 1978, and so he leapt at the BBWAA’s invitation to present Cole with the prestigious hardware
item.content:encoded:
Clad in a black tux and a matching bowtie, Ron Guidry stepped to the podium at the New York Hilton Midtown on Jan. 27, 2024 to recognize a fellow Yankee and to pass a torch.
Speaking at the Baseball Writers’ Association of America Awards Dinner in his Louisiana drawl, “Gator” introduced Gerrit Cole, voted the American League’s Cy Young for 2023. Guidry won the same award while wearing pinstripes back in 1978, and so he leapt at the BBWAA’s invitation to present Cole with the prestigious hardware.
Cole called it a “really special” moment with an “integral part of the organization,” as Guidry took him under his wing after he signed with the Yankees before the 2020 season.
“They called and asked, and I said, ‘Sure, I’d be honored to go give it to him,’” Guidry recently told the Daily News. “And it would be nice if Cam would do the same thing with Gerrit.”
By “Cam,” Guidry meant Cam Schlittler, who is poised to become the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young and the first since Cole. The 25-year-old has been so stellar that Aaron Boone recently lobbied for the MVP Award, though Schlittler isn’t seen as a frontrunner for that trophy.
“He’s a stud,” the manager said.
With Schlittler set to make his 33rd and final regular season start against the Rays on Thursday, the right-hander is 14-6 with an American League-leading 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts over 190.2 innings. In just his first full big league season, he has put together one of the best campaigns by a Yankees starter in franchise history.
Guidry’s 1978 season is widely considered the best. No one is going to match his 25-3 record, nine shutouts or 273.2 innings that year, not with the way the sport has changed.
“Just a different game of baseball back then. It’s just not the same as it is now,” Schlittler said. “No one’s throwing that many innings. So he’s a legend for a reason.”
“He’s going to have to play hell to try to break my shutout record,” Guidry added with a laugh.
With a 1.74 ERA in 1978, Guidry is one of just two Yankees starters who have logged at least 30 starts and finished a season with a sub-2.00 ERA since earned runs became an official stat. Spud Chandler, who had a 1.64 ERA in 1943, is the other. Schlittler is trying to become the third.
Guidry also struck out 248 batters in 1978, a Yankees record at the time. Cole toppled him with 257 punchies in 2022.
An ace long before analytics became commonplace in baseball, Guidry also had a 9.1 fWAR in 1978, a record for Yankees pitchers. His 2.19 FIP ranks fifth behind a few guys who pitched in the early 1900s.
Like some of Guidry’s surface numbers, those stats easily outpace Schlittler’s still-sensational production; he leads all AL starters with a 6.1 fWAR. His 2.57 FIP that ranks second.
Regardless, Guidry is delighted that their names keep getting mentioned side by side.
“It’s always a compliment when somebody today is compared to somebody from yesterday,” the 76-year-old said. “It just so happens if you’re talking about Cam, you’re talking to me.
“That’s a compliment to me.”
Schlittler and Guidry haven’t gotten to know each other too well, but they have crossed paths since the former started showing up to big league camp two springs ago. Guidry is a frequent guest instructor, watching bullpens, parting his wisdom, and answering any questions the pinstripers’ new generation of pitchers may have.
Even two springs ago, months before Schlittler debuted, Guidry saw the makings of a future ace.
“You could see that there’s something there,” Guidry said.
Since then, Schlittler has bulked up, increased his velocity, cemented himself in Yankees postseason lore, and turned into the nastiest pitcher in a rotation that also features Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.
He’s also established himself as a rather competitive individual, whether it be between the lines or while beefing with rival fans on social media.
“He’s got that air about him. That, ‘I’m good, come get me,’” said Guidry, who has watched Schlittler quite a bit this year. “You’ve shown them that you have the stuff and you’re not afraid to throw it.”
The stuff Guidry mentioned is typically coming in hot.
With a four-seamer, a cutter and a sinker, Schlittler throws some variation of a fastball roughly 90% of the time, making his rise all the more impressive and unique. His four-seamer, meanwhile, averaged 98 mph entering Thursday’s game.
“You marvel at his fastball because he throws in excess of 100 miles per hour. Well, when you can throw that hard, you have a big advantage over a lot of hitters,” Guidry said, though he would like to see Schlittler develop some secondary stuff as he advances in his career.
Schlittler throws a curveball that grades out rather well, but he’s thrown it less than 10% of the time. He has also thrown a slider and previously toyed with a changeup and a splitter.
“At some point in his career, he’s going to have to start looking at something else to complement that because he’s not going to be able to stand up to the strain of throwing that hard for 20 years,” Guidry continued. “It might be 10 years, but it’s not going to be for 20 years. Even Nolan [Ryan] slowed up to 98 when he was 40 years old.”
While Guidry fired with his left arm during an entirely different era, he said that his prime self and Schlittler are “basically the same.” He noted that “we’re considered power pitchers” — though Guidry relied heavily on a fastball-slider combo — and that his Cy Young season was his first as a full-time starter in the majors.
Guidry began 1977 in the bullpen but began his run as a rotation staple by mid-May that year.
Now Guidry would like to see Schlittler join him on the short list of Yankees pitchers who have won the award.
“Any time a Yankee is in that position, you’re pulling for him,” Guidry said. “Because it don’t happen often.”

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Giancarlo Stanton, Carlos Lagrange, Game 1 starter among Yankees’ many playoff puzzle pieces
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while. “There’s a lot
item.content:encoded:
The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while.
“There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days,” the manager said before the Yankees played the division-winning Rays on Wednesday. “Hopefully, we have a lot of options to choose from.”
THE RETURN OF STANTON (AND GRISHAM)?
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 due to three separate calf strains (two right, one left), and Trent Grisham, sidelined by his second right hamstring strain of the season, took live at-bats in Somerset on Wednesday. Both ran the bases, and Boone said Stanton homered while getting six or seven at-bats.
“They’re knocking on the door,” Boone said, but he wasn’t sure if Stanton, a decorated postseason performer, could be ready for the Wild Card round.
The manager previously said that Grisham could be in play, though he wasn’t expected to be activated before the final five games of the regular season.
Asked what he would need to see from Stanton after a five-month layoff, Boone earnestly said, “I’m not sure.”
“I don’t know that answer,” he continued. “Obviously, there’ll be conversations with him. Does he fit on the roster? Is it realistic? All those things, and I can’t answer that right now.”
With the Yankees already log-jammed with first-base/DH types — Stanton can’t play the outfield anymore — Boone added that the former MVP would probably be used as a pinch-hitter, if anything. While not a big role, Stanton’s right-handed bat could be helpful off the bench if the Yankees face the lefty-heavy Red Sox, their likeliest opponent, in the Wild Card round.
Grisham, meanwhile, would give the Yankees an interesting choice in center field with Spencer Jones handling the position in his absence. Jones has outperformed Grisham at the plate, but both are shaky defenders, and the latter has postseason experience that the rookie does not.
LAGRANGE TO DEBUT?
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said of flamethrowing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange, who threw live batting practice on Wednesday.
But the skipper noted that a lot of “unknown” comes with righty, who has yet to make his major league debut, only recently returned from a shoulder sprain, and has just eight relief appearances under his belt this season. If the Yankees were to use Lagrange and his 100-plus-mph fastball, it would be out of the bullpen.
Asked why the Yankees don’t just promote Lagrange now, Boone said that they still have to cover innings over the last few games of the regular season. They would also have to clear space for him on the 40-man and active rosters.
While Lagrange is 23 and Stanton is 36, both are in similar positions in that they offer the Yankees an intriguing combination of upside, mystery and risk. Asked how Boone might personally weigh all that as the Yankees prepare to make their postseason roster, he said the club will “make the best decision possible” “if those guys are truly pushing into the conversation.”
“Carlos is in the stay ready [phase]. G [got] at-bats today,” Boone said. “All, at least, putting them on the outskirts of the conversation, if nothing else.”
WHO STARTS GAME 1?
Cam Schlittler is the clear frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award. So he’s obviously going to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round, right?
“Not necessarily,” Boone said. “We’ll see. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 doesn’t affect the next series. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 can pitch Game 2 and Game 5 in the next series, for example. We’ll decide what makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games.”
Gerrit Cole, who totaled two earned runs, three walks and eight strikeouts over 5.2 innings and 105 pitches on Wednesday against the Rays, is currently lined up for Game 1 of the Wild Card round on extra rest. The 2023 Cy Young winner, now 22 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, has struggled to get swing-and-miss this season. He’s also faltered against the Red Sox throughout his career. With Max Fried and Carlos Rodón also in the rotation, the case can be made that Cole has been the Yankees’ fourth-best starter lately.
Schlittler, who dominated Boston in last year’s Wild Card series, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1. He is scheduled to make his final start of the regular season on Thursday.
VOLPE AT THIRD? MCMAHON OFF THE ROSTER?
With the lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon putting the finishing touches on an abysmal offensive season and taking a step back defensively, the righty-hitting Anthony Volpe did some pregame work at third base on Wednesday. Boone expects the shortstop turned second baseman to play the hot corner in one or two games before the regular season ends.
“Good to go,” Volpe, who played a few games at third in the minors this year, said of his comfort level at the position.
Meanwhile, José Caballero, another righty, has already gotten some starts at third over McMahon against right-handed pitching. If Volpe shows that he can handle third, it could increase the odds of the Yankees leaving McMahon off their Wild Card roster.
Boone said that he still sees McMahon as a “top-shelf” defender, but he entered Wednesday’s game with -2 Defensive Runs Saved and one Out Above Average, numbers well below career norms. Couple that with a 73 wRC+, and the $16 million man has not been a quality player, though he did hit a grand slam on Wednesday.
“I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I want him in the game and the ball hit to him in a big spot,” Boone said. “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half and lately getting it going. But through his struggles that he’s had offensively, he’s gotten a lot of big hits for us, too, along the way.”
On the subject of third base, Boone also said that he hasn’t given much thought to Jazz Chisholm Jr. trying the position again. However, he’s not ruling it out.
WHAT ABOUT OTHER INJURED ARMS?
Fernando Cruz made a rather adamant appearance in the Yankees’ clubhouse on Wednesday. The reliever, out with a partially torn UCL, repeatedly said that he refused to “accept” the diagnosis.
“I had real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” said Cruz, who isn’t considering surgery right now. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart, it’s not a partial tear.”
While it seems rather improbable that Cruz will pitch again this season, he said that that is his goal, and Boone didn’t rule out the possibility. The righty threw a touch-and-feel bullpen three days ago, and he plans to throw another bullpen on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Clarke Schmidt felt better playing catch on Wednesday than he did on Tuesday after experiencing some biceps cramping over the weekend. However, if the recently returned Tommy John patient is not a viable option by Thursday, “then we’ll probably go a different way,” Boone said, referring to the Yankees’ postseason roster plans.
Finally, Ryan Weathers isn’t expected to throw live batting practice until sometime during the Wild Card series, so he won’t be an option.
With Weathers ruled out and Schmidt’s status uncertain, it will be interesting to see how the Yankees fill out their Wild Card bullpen. On a related note, Boone said that he sees “no scenario” in which the team carries 13 pitchers for the series. They may not even roster 12, he said with so many balls up in the air.
“It depends who’s available and who’s not,” Boone said.

item.title: [el-balad.com] Rays clinch AL East title for the first time since 2021 as Yankees head to the wild-card round — Rays Vs Yankees now has a very different edge - El-Balad.com
item.dc:creator: Chris Lawson
item.description: This was the kind of Tuesday that changes the entire shape of a postseason race. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East, secured a first-round bye, and suddenly made the Yankees’ path look a lot harder than it did 24 hours earlier. item.content:encoded:
This was the kind of Tuesday that changes the entire shape of a postseason race. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East, secured a first-round bye, and suddenly made the Yankees’ path look a lot harder than it did 24 hours earlier. For New York, the comfort of having already locked up a postseason berth now comes with a much less comfortable reality: the wild-card round is next.
The Rays finishing on top of the division is not a small footnote. It is the difference between waiting with an advantage and scrambling for survival. Tampa Bay had not won the American League East since 2021, and now it has done it again with the sort of timing that makes the whole thing feel like a statement. The Rays are not just in the playoff picture. They are positioned to matter immediately.
New York got the result, but Tampa Bay got the prize
The Yankees did win Game 1 of the doubleheader, 2-0, behind eight shutout innings from Carlos Rodon, and that should not be ignored. This is still a team that can point to its starting pitching and say, with some justification, that it remains a dangerous opponent in the American League. But that is the problem with baseball’s playoff ladder: one good result does not erase the bigger picture.
Because while New York was grinding through nearly 13 hours at Yankee Stadium, the Rays were doing the one thing that actually mattered most. They beat Max Fried in the nightcap and then walked away as AL East champions. That changes everything. Tampa Bay gets the first-round bye and the cleaner route. New York gets a tougher road and less margin for error.
Jose Caballero summed up the mood perfectly after the clinch. “The 162 first games, it doesn’t matter,” he said. “Now, the clock starts.” That is exactly the point. The regular season can fill the calendar, build the record and create the noise, but once the division is decided, all of that fades. What matters now is who gets the privilege of choosing a better route and who has to fight through the mess.
For the Yankees, the answer is simple enough: they have work to do, and they will have to do it without Aaron Judge for at least the AL wild card series against the Boston Red Sox. That is not a detail. That is a major complication. It leaves New York leaning even more heavily on the very thing that has kept them in the conversation all along: the starting pitching.
So yes, the Yankees can still be taken seriously as a possible team to beat in the American League. But the Rays have made the bigger move, and in October that is often the only move that really counts. Tampa Bay are AL East champions. New York are in the wild-card round. That is the difference between control and uncertainty, and on Tuesday the Rays grabbed all of it.

item.content:encoded:
This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more.
Ronald Acuña Jr. of the Braves may be hitting .259 with career lows in exit velocity and hard-hit rate, but don’t be fooled by the overall stats. If the star outfielder can fight through a left shin contusion he suffered Tuesday night on a foul ball at the plate—he’s currently considered day-to-day—he’ll be a force to be reckoned with in October. Ever since mid-August when Acuña began to knock off the rust from two IL stints, he’s been a dangerous, dynamic hitter.
The tell-tale sign is how Acuña is getting to high fastballs he used to miss.
| Acuna vs. 95+ MPH | No. | BA | SLG | HR | Attack Angle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Through Aug. 22 | 315 | .183 | .268 | 1 | 9° |
| Since | 119 | .393 | .857 | 4 | 7° |
Pitchers were dominating Acuña with velocity over his hands. No more. Acuña has made the adjustment. While his barrel had been working underneath the pitch plane, now he is flattening his attack angle, as you can see here:
Acuña heads my list of hitters who are most likely to cap a disappointing year with a strong finish.
Down Year but Primed for Big October
1. Ronald Acuña Jr., Braves
2. Mookie Betts, Dodgers
3. Will Smith, Dodgers
4. Trevor Story, Red Sox
5. José Ramírez, Guardians
Gerrit Cole, Game 2 Starter?
Yankees righthander Gerrit Cole broke through a late-season slump with an improved outing Friday in Arizona (six innings, two earned runs).
As I said last week here, Cole has been throwing too many strikes in the middle of the plate. His fix: tighten the delivery to be more compact and move almost six inches on the rubber toward the third base side.
A frequent tinkerer, Cole began the season toward the center of the rubber but after the Red Sox pounded him for four runs June 27, he moved to the first base side July 3 and stayed there for 13 starts. But after his poor start Sept. 12 against the Mets, which included a career high of hard hits, he returned to the center.
Here you can see his foot position change on the rubber in his past two starts:
It’s the quickest fix to a command issue. You don’t need to change mechanics, just the lane in which the ball leaves your hand.
How did it work? His command was much better. Look at his fastball heat maps and it’s clear he did a better job of keeping the ball out of the center lane:
Cole Fastball Heat Maps
This start moved Cole closer to getting the ball ahead of Max Fried or Carlos Rodon (or both) in a wild-card series against Boston.
As usual, Cole pounded the zone. He has not issued a walk among 71 batters faced in his past three starts. But still a concern: the swing-and-miss still has not returned to his game. He had only six swings-and-misses against Arizona. His September whiff rate is 17%, down from 22.4% entering the month.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have a difficult decision in choosing who starts after Schlittler, a decision that should be based on how Cole, Fried and Rodon are throwing the ball rather than sheer numbers or opponent trends. The Red Sox are slightly better against left-handed pitching (24–15, .746 OPS) than right-handed (60–55, .713 OPS), though the return of Roman Anthony changes that a bit.
📺 TV on TV This Week
Sunday, Sept. 27: Postseason Preview, 8 p.m. ET (MLB Network)
Up to 53 pressure-packed games in 33 days. The best month in all of sports is just about here.
I’ll’ll also be recording a playoff preview show on Monday along with MLB editor Will Laws and staff writer Ryan Phillips. Look out for that on our
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [heavy.com] Aaron Boone Drops Surprising Cam Schlittler Revelation Ahead of Yankees' Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: Zach Kaplan
item.description: Cam Schlittler may have the American League Cy Young locked up, but that doesn’t mean he’ll be toeing the slab in the first game of the Yankees’ upcoming Wild Card series. On Wednesday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone dropped a few surprising tidbits, including that ailing sluggers Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham might be back in pinstripes soon, and that the Yankees are considering adding top pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange to the postseason roster despite Lagrange not having made his debut y
item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler may have the American League Cy Young locked up, but that doesn’t mean he’ll be toeing the slab in the first game of the Yankees’ upcoming Wild Card series.
On Wednesday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone dropped a few surprising tidbits, including that ailing sluggers Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham might be back in pinstripes soon, and that the Yankees are considering adding top pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange to the postseason roster despite Lagrange not having made his debut yet.
Still, the most surprising part of Boone’s pregame press conference might have been his response to the question of which Yankees starter would start Game 1 of the American League Wild Card on Tuesday night.
“We’ll see. Not necessarily,” Boone said about Schlittler, noting that much of his decision around Schlittler’s first start will depend on how they feel about a potential ALDS pitching order.
Cam Schlittler’s Cy Young Caliber Season
Not only does it look Schlittler’s first full professional season will culminate in an American League Cy Young award, but it’s nothing short of historic. Earlier in the year, Schlittler posted a 1.14 ERA in his first 16 road starts of the season, which broke the all-time American League record. With a solid start against the Rays Thursday night, Schlittler would finish his season with a sub-2 ERA, and become the first Yankee to do so since Ron Guidry in his 1978 Cy Young season.
If the Yankees match up against the Red Sox next week, which seems more than likely, Schlittler will get another chance to draw ire from his childhood team after ending their season as a rookie in Game 3 of last year’s Wild Card.
Schlittler also has some history of his own that he can chase, with a little help from the rest of the team. He enters Thursday’s start with 22 straight road starts in which he has recorded more strikeouts than hits allowed, a streak that continued with his six strikeouts to three hits against the Diamondbacks. Only Randy Johnson has had more consecutive starts, doing so in 23 straight road appearances between 1999 and 2000.
Schlittler wouldn’t get another opportunity to do so unless he starts at Tropicana Field in a potential ALDS game with the Yankees. Being put in a group that includes Randy Johnson would be the icing on the cake to an elite first full campaign.
Aaron Boone’s Cam Schlittler Decision
Yankees manager Aaron Boone will have his hands full deciding which order to send out his four top starters next week, as one wrong move could be what ends the Yankees’ season far short of their ultimate goal.
Max Fried and Schlittler will likely be the two choices for Game 1, and Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon would be the choices for an if-necessary Game 3 to decide the season. But for Boone, and all Yankee fans at home, the hope is that they won’t need to go there.
With a strong start from Fried or Schlittler, and a bullpen that looks even more formidable with a potential new, young back-end reliever in Lagrange, the Yankees could be well-positioned for a Wild Card triumph after Tuesday night.

item.title: [bolavip.com] NY Yankees’ Max Fried sounds off on Rays celebrating AL East title at Yankee Stadium

Now locked into the Wild Card Round, the New York Yankees are shifting their focus to the postseason, where starting pitcher Max Fried addressed the sting of watching a division rival celebrate on Bronx turf. “You don’t want anyone to be celebrating at your stadium,” Fried told the YES Network following the game. “Especially this morning, with the
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are the newly crowned American League East champions, clinching a first-round bye as they await the winner of the Wild Card Series. Now locked into the Wild Card Round, the New York Yankees are shifting their focus to the postseason, where starting pitcher Max Fried addressed the sting of watching a division rival celebrate on Bronx turf.
“You don’t want anyone to be celebrating at your stadium,” Fried told the YES Network following the game. “Especially this morning, with the way Carlos came out, we wanted to put some pressure on and win some games. Unfortunately, I wasn’t able to follow up what he did this afternoon.”
Fried was blunt about his own performance during the nightcap of Tuesday’s doubleheader. Though Carlos Rodon turned in a gem during his final regular-season start, the Yankees couldn’t complete the sweep, leaving the door open for Tampa Bay to seal the division title.
Looking ahead to the road to October, manager Aaron Boone outlined the team’s strategy for the remaining five games of the regular season. However, Boone also delivered a concerning injury update regarding Aaron Judge, clouding the captain’s availability for the upcoming Wild Card Series.
Max Fried #54 of the New York Yankees throws a live bullpen session.
Fried struggles against Rays’ offense
Tuesday presented a tale of two games for New York’s rotation. Game 1 saw Rodon deliver a dominant performance on the mound to reach the 100-strikeout mark for the season, but Fried was unable to replicate that command in the second matchup.
Fried allowed four earned runs on six hits over 6.2 innings as Tampa Bay pulled away for a 6-1 victory. The sub-par outing highlighted pressing questions about the rotation’s consistency, especially with no margin for error in a short Wild Card Series where a single loss can alter the entire series.
Fried maintains confidence in Yankees’ rotation
Despite his rough outing, Fried expressed full confidence in his fellow rotation members as the postseason approaches. “We’ve got great arms. We’ve got a guy who’s going to win the Cy Young. Anytime you have that guy in your rotation, it’s obviously a good thing. We’ve got a lot of guys throwing the ball really well right now,” Fried remarked.
Key takeaways
- The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East division title and celebrated at Yankee Stadium.
- Max Fried allowed four earned runs over 6.2 innings in a 6-1 defeat, and sounded off on Rays’ celebration.
- The starting pitcher expressed full confidence in New York’s rotation ahead of the postseason.
SurveyDo you think Fried can bounce back in the postseason?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Are About To Make Huge Mistake With Gerrit Cole
item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: The New York Yankees now know that they will have to play in a best-of-three Wild Card Series in the Bronx starting on Tuesday. Gerrit Cole is set to pitch on Wednesday against the Tampa Bay Rays, and that would put him on five days of rest before the Wild Card Series starts. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees now know that they will have to play in a best-of-three Wild Card Series in the Bronx starting on Tuesday.
Gerrit Cole is set to pitch on Wednesday against the Tampa Bay Rays, and that would put him on five days of rest before the Wild Card Series starts. Cam Schlittler will pitch on Thursday, giving him four days of rest if the Yankees plan to start him in Game 1.
Schlittler has had no problems working on four days of rest this season, so he should still draw the Game 1 start. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón both pitched on Tuesday, so assuming neither one makes another traditional start in the regular season, both would be available to pitch in the Wild Card Series with some extra rest.
Essentially the Yankees have to decide whether to start Cole or Rodón as the third starter in a Wild Card Series, assuming Fried and Schlittler both get starts. Aaron Boone has already noted that fans should expect Cole to get a start in the Wild Card Series, and judging by how things are lining up, that start could come in Game 1 or 2. He would be going into Game 1 with five days of rest, setting Schlittler up to pitch in Game 2 on five days of rest if the Yankees want to make sure he doesn't pitch on four days' rest.
Then, Fried or Rodón would start Game 3 with extended rest. It's safe to assume that if one of them starts in the regular season finale, the other would start Game 3 on extended rest. However, the reality is, starting Cole over either of them is a mistake.
Cole has a 5.34 ERA this month and also struggles against the Red Sox. Since 2020, when Cole joined the Yankees, he has had a 5.93 ERA against the Red Sox in the regular season. In his postseason career, he has faced the Red Sox twice, allowing seven runs in eight innings.
Fans already know how god Fried and Schlittler are, and they both deserve to start. However, Rodón should be the one getting the nod over Cole in a best-of-three series against the Red Sox. Rodón has a 1.89 ERA since returning from the injured list in August. He has delivered three straight quality starts, and the Yankees should ride the hot hand.
More MLB: How Can Dodgers Legally Get Josue De Paula On Postseason Roster?
